[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced Ruby on Rails: Metaprogramming and Reflection"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Metaprogramming and reflection are powerful features of Ruby that Ruby on Rails heavily relies on under the hood. Reflection allows code to inspect itself and its environment at runtime, while metaprogramming enables code to write or modify other code dynamically. Mastering these concepts allows you to write highly DRY, flexible, and expressive Rails applications."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Reflection in Ruby"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Reflection is the ability of a computer program to examine, introspect, and modify its own structure and behavior at runtime. In Ruby, almost everything is an object, which makes reflection exceptionally powerful."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"user = User.new
# Inspecting methods and ancestors
puts user.class.ancestors
puts user.methods.include?(:save)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Reflection Methods in Active Record"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Rails extends Ruby's built-in reflection capabilities extensively in Active Record. You can query models about their database columns, associations, and reflections dynamically."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"User.column_names returns an array of all column names as strings."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"User.reflect_on_all_associations returns metadata regarding model relationships like belongs_to and has_many."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"# Finding all associations of a model dynamically
User.reflect_on_all_associations.each do |association|
  puts "Association Name: #{association.name}, Type: #{association.macro}"
end"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Metaprogramming"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Metaprogramming is writing code that writes code. In Ruby, this is typically achieved using dynamic method definition, dynamic method invocation via send, and hooks like inherited or included."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Using define_method"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Instead of writing repetitive boilerplate methods, you can iterate over a collection and define methods dynamically at runtime using define_method."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"class DynamicAttributeChecker
  ['admin', 'moderator', 'guest'].each do |role|
    define_method("is_#{role}?") do
      self.role == role
    end
  end

  attr_accessor :role
end

user = DynamicAttributeChecker.new
user.role = 'admin'
puts user.is_admin? # Output: true
puts user.is_guest? # Output: false"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Method Missing and Respond_to_missing?"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a method is called on an object that does not exist, Ruby invokes method_missing. Rails uses this pattern extensively (for example, dynamic finders like find_by_email_and_name)."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"class FlexibleConfig
  def initialize
    @settings = {}
  end

  def method_missing(name, *args, &block)
    if name.to_s.end_with?('=')
      key = name.to_s.chomp('=').to_sym
      @settings[key] = args.first
    else
      @settings[name]
    end
  end

  def respond_to_missing?(name, include_private = false)
    true
  end
end"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Performance Considerations"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always implement respond_to_missing? when overriding method_missing to maintain proper object introspection."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Prefer define_method over method_missing when possible because defined methods are faster and easier to debug."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid excessive metaprogramming if standard object-oriented design patterns can solve the problem more readably."}]
